summary:
Jujuy stands under Argentina's national framework, and no Jujuy-specific statute, court ruling or enforcement incident was identified in the source inventory. The national layer applies in full: Law 26.743 permits legal gender change without surgery, hormones or judicial approval, and Decree 476/2021 requires the third gender marker X on national identity cards and passports.

An April 2025 Washington Blade report datelined Buenos Aires states that the Milei-era national framework applies to all provinces including Jujuy: a decree of 5 February 2025 restricted minors' access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone treatment (a Federal Court subsequently ruled the ban unconstitutional in April 2025, restoring access nationwide), trans people hired under the 1% public-sector Trans Labor Quota were dismissed, and the federal anti-discrimination agency INADI was abolished.

The same report records activists' testimony that police violence, already common against trans and travesti sex workers, has worsened and is worst outside Buenos Aires, naming Jujuy among the more conservative interior provinces where the situation is reported as more acute. This is the only Jujuy-specific signal in the inventory: an activist characterisation of provincial conditions rather than a documented incident with date and outcome.

Nationally the hate-crime picture is severe. Agencia Presentes reported on 19 March 2026 that the national observatory recorded 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity in 2025, a 62% rise year on year and a ten-year record, averaging one every 38 hours. Perpetrators were mostly security-force personnel and unknown assailants in public space; beatings were the main modality; institutional violence rose from 17 cases in 2024 to 64 in 2025; 32% of 2025 incidents occurred in police stations or prisons; and 43% of perpetrators were strangers to their victims.

Jujuy has no local reporting infrastructure to generate separate records, so the province's own incidence cannot be isolated from the national figures above.
tangentialFactors:
Activists interviewed in April 2025 described the interior provinces, Jujuy included, as more conservative than Buenos Aires, which shapes expectations about social hostility independently of the written law.

The abolition of INADI in February 2024 removed the national complaints channel that a visitor or resident would otherwise use to report discrimination, leaving provincial mechanisms as the only remaining route; the inventory does not describe what Jujuy itself provides.

Nationally, Penal Code Article 80(4) as amended in 2012 imposes life imprisonment for homicide motivated by hatred based on gender identity or expression, but on 5 April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the removal of the travesticidio aggravating circumstance in the Gabriel Marino case, so the gender-motivated aggravator is currently not applied there.
localsOnly:
Residents of Jujuy are covered by the national Gender Identity Law 26.743 for legal gender, name and image changes on the civil registry, and by the third gender marker X on national identity cards and passports under Decree 476/2021.

The February 2025 decree on housing transgender people in prisons applies nationally; its operative terms are not provided by the sources, so how Jujuy's prisons implement it is unresolved.

Trans workers dismissed from national public-sector posts under the Trans Labor Quota cuts affect residents of Jujuy employed in national bodies, per the April 2025 Washington Blade report.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Jujuy provincial law, provincial court decision, provincial hate-crime statistic or named local incident appears in the inventory; the province-specific content rests on one activist characterisation reported in April 2025 and on the absence of local recording infrastructure.

Whether Jujuy province maintains its own anti-discrimination body, its own hate-crime recording, or any provincial variation in the application of Law 26.743 is not sourced here and remains unresolved.

The inventory does not document airport or border screening practice at Jujuy's entry points, nor any facility-access dispute within the province.
